Let me now construct a case designed to maximize the number of *surviving* clauses (to stress the universe-falsification step). I want many minimal hitting sets. Let me design:

Training windows: 10000 windows. Predicates: 32. I want many minimal hitting sets of size ≤ 4.

Idea: make predicate p_i true on a set of training windows such that minimal hitting sets are numerous. E.g., with training windows w_1..w_32, let p_i be true only on w_i. Then the minimal hitting sets are the singletons {p_i} (32 of them) — condition 1 requires hitting all 32 windows → only singletons... wait, {p_i} doesn't hit all windows. A clause must hit EVERY training window. With p_i true only on w_i, a clause must contain all 32 predicates to cover all windows → but then minimality fails (removing any leaves uncovered windows? no — minimality requires the clause to become FALSE on some window, i.e., some window where all remaining literals are false; with p_i true only on w_i, removing p_j from the full set leaves w_j uncovered → false → so the full 32-set IS minimal, but its length is 32 > width).

To have many clauses of size ≤4 each hitting all windows: e.g., 4 groups of windows, where each predicate is true on one window from each group... Let me think of the classic: windows w_1..w_4 (4 windows); predicate p_j true on windows {w_j, w_{j+1}} (cyclic) → minimal hitting sets of size 2: {p_1,p_3}, {p_2,p_4}. Not many.

Alternative: use 32 predicates where p_i is true on window set S_i = {w_1..w_4} \ {w_i mod 4}... 

Honestly, the number of clauses surviving conditions 1&2 is what matters. Let me just measure the worst case with an adversarial construction: predicates = all 4-subsets? We only have 32 predicates.

Consider: 4 training windows w1..w4. For each 4-subset... hmm, with 32 predicates we can have at most 32 distinct truth patterns over 4 windows (2^4=16 patterns). Clauses must hit all 4 windows, and be minimal.

With 4 windows and 16 possible patterns, using 32 predicates (duplicates of patterns), the minimal hitting sets: each clause is minimal if for each literal p in it, there's a window where all others are false.

Let's construct: for each window w (4 windows) and each subset T of the other 3 windows, a predicate with truth pattern = {w} ∪ T. Then a clause is minimal iff... this can produce many minimal hitting sets.

Let me just try a random-ish adversarial construction and measure the time; if the time stays reasonable (a few seconds), we're fine.

Actually, let me directly measure the cost of the enumeration phase itself with 32 predicates and width 4: 41448 subsets, each with big-int ops. That's the dominant fixed cost. Let me time just the enumeration with a trivial setup.

Let me instrument: build 32 predicates where the training masks are random (so most clauses fail condition 1 early), and measure enumerate_clauses time.

Let me test with random bool vectors of length 10000 for train and 65536 for universe.
